item.title: Fijian couple leaving NZ with their newborn baby and a $32k hospital bill
item.description: A couple who welcomed the arrival of their second child two months ago have received a hospital bill for nearly $32,000. The healthy 3.2kg baby boy arrived via C-section at Dunedin Hospital on June 27, three days after his parents’ work visas – and their access to New Zealand’s publicly funded healthcare – had expired.
item.content:encoded:
A couple who welcomed the arrival of their second child two months ago have received a hospital bill for nearly $32,000.

The healthy 3.2kg baby boy arrived via C-section at Dunedin Hospital on June 27, three days after his parents’ work visas – and their access to New Zealand’s publicly funded healthcare – had expired.

His father Shalveen Sen, his mother Swastikha Chand, and his older brother, aged six, arrived in the country three years ago from Fiji.

Sen worked as a commercial cleaner, while Chand worked as a caregiver, but their work experience – and job offers – were not enough for Immigration New Zealand (INZ) to renew their work visas.

The couple had been trying to renew those visas, initially issued for three years, over the past year. The stress over their immigration status was compounded by the news they had a baby due in early July.

Chand also experienced pregnancy complications, which led to medical advice for her not to travel in the third trimester.

The couple’s midwife informed them a birth that wasn’t covered by the public system would cost around $9000.

INZ advise those who were not eligible for publicly funded healthcare must bear the costs themselves. Those in that position “must show you have a minimum of NZ$9000 to pay for your maternity care,” the agency says.

Chand, who delivered her son via C-section, was in Dunedin Hospital for three days and two nights, with both mother and son doing well – but the bill ended up totalling $31,815.50.

An invoice from Te Whatu Ora Southern, dated August 24, noted that the two night stay on the inpatient ward cost $3375.66, while the C-Section cost $24,289.99, along with GST of $4149.85.

Sen said it had been a stressful time for the family, who were now unable to work, as they did not have valid visas.

“We are out of options,” he said. “We’ve been struggling for two months now.”

The family was overstaying and had to leave New Zealand. They were awaiting the arrival of their baby’s passport from Fiji, and were set to return to the island nation on Sunday.

Sen said he set up a fundraiser to help pay the hospital bill, as the family would struggle to manage it on their own when back in Fiji, which they had left three years ago after selling their assets.

“That is impossible for us to pay,” he said.

It was a particularly difficult situation for their older son, Sen added, as “he doesn’t know anything about Fiji now”.

item.title: TAANZ welcomes Fiji tourism tax exemption
item.description: The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has welcomed the Fijian Government’s decision to exempt existing bookings from the new five per cent Tourism Services Tax, saying it provides much-needed certainty for Kiwi travellers. The TST will now apply only to new bookings made on or after September 1, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has welcomed the Fijian Government’s decision to exempt existing bookings from the new five per cent Tourism Services Tax, saying it provides much-needed certainty for Kiwi travellers.

The TST will now apply only to new bookings made on or after September 1, 2026.

Bookings made before September 1 will not attract the tax, even when the holiday or tourism service takes place after that date.

TAANZ chief executive Julie White described the decision as practical and sensible, particularly for New Zealanders who had already booked and paid for Fiji holidays.

“This gives Kiwi travellers the certainty they needed,” Ms White said.

“Those who made their bookings before 1 September can now travel knowing they will not face an unexpected additional tax on an existing booking.”

Ms White said TAANZ had never opposed Fiji’s right to introduce the tax, but had raised concerns about its proposed application to existing bookings, the short implementation period and uncertainty for travellers and the travel industry.

“We are therefore very pleased the Fijian Government has listened to the concerns raised by the tourism and travel sectors and adopted a practical transition approach,” she said.

Ms White said Fiji remained one of the most popular overseas destinations for New Zealand travellers, supported by strong aviation connections and close cultural and family ties.

“New Zealanders love travelling to Fiji. It is a destination people return to time and again for its people, hospitality, beaches and the ease of getting there from New Zealand,” she said.

TAANZ also acknowledged discussions between Government and tourism and travel industry representatives that led to the revised implementation arrangements.

“This is a good example of what can be achieved when government and industry listen to each other and work through the practical impacts of a policy,” Ms White said.

The five per cent TST will apply to qualifying tourism services and operators for new bookings from September 1 and is scheduled to remain in effect until August 31, 2027.

“Today’s announcement removes a significant area of uncertainty and is a positive outcome for travellers, travel businesses and Fiji’s tourism industry,” Ms White said.

item.title: Taiwan foreign minister to attend Pacific islands leaders summit events
item.description: Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung will attend events related to a major summit of leaders from Pacific islands nations in Palau starting next week, his office said on Wednesday, though China said he had no right to take part. China’s test-firing in July of a missile into the Pacific alarmed regional powers but failed to spur a unified response from Pacific Island governments, underscoring divi
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung will attend events related to a major summit of leaders from Pacific islands nations in Palau starting next week, his office said on Wednesday, though China said he had no right to take part.

China’s test-firing in July of a missile into the Pacific alarmed regional powers but failed to spur a unified response from Pacific Island governments, underscoring divisions over how to confront growing strategic competition in the region.

China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific island countries with formal ties to Taipei, with only three remaining – Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands.

Taiwan’s foreign ministry said that Lin would leave for Palau on Thursday and be there for a week, taking part in side events to the summit, including a Pacific Islands Forum dialogue meeting hosted by the forum’s secretariat, and the Pacific Prosperity Exhibit.

Lin will also meet Taiwan’s Pacific diplomatic allies and “other friendly nations to exchange views on deepening the partnership between Taiwan and Pacific island nations, as well as jointly maintaining peace, stability and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region,” the ministry said in a statement.

China says Taiwan is one of its provinces, not a country.

Beijing’s foreign ministry said Taipei had “no qualifications” to take part in the forum, which is being held from Sunday until September 4.

“The Taiwan authorities sending Lin Chia-lung and other Taiwan independence separatists scurrying about all over to curry favour is a futile attempt to grab attention,” it said in a statement sent to Reuters.

The forum’s Fiji-based secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Chinese comments.

China has expanded its influence in the Pacific in recent years through infrastructure financing, diplomatic outreach and security cooperation, which has prompted concern among traditional partners including Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

item.title: Fiji Airways gets broader US operating rights
item.description: Fiji Airways has received immediate approval from the United States Department of Transportation to expand its scheduled and charter operating authority in the US, giving the national carrier greater flexibility for future services. The authorization allows Fiji Airways broader rights to operate passenger, cargo and mail services to and from the United States while its amended foreign air carrier
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways has received immediate approval from the United States Department of Transportation to expand its scheduled and charter operating authority in the US, giving the national carrier greater flexibility for future services.

The authorization allows Fiji Airways broader rights to operate passenger, cargo and mail services to and from the United States while its amended foreign air carrier permit continues through the regulatory approval process.

The authority will remain valid for two years.

While the decision does not introduce any new Fiji Airways routes, it removes a regulatory hurdle that could make future expansion in the US market easier.

US authorities determined that Fiji Airways satisfied the necessary financial and operational requirements and remained substantially owned and effectively controlled by Fijian interests.

No objections were filed during the review, allowing the authorization to take effect immediately.

Despite securing the expanded rights, Fiji Airways has not announced any additional US destinations.

The airline currently connects Fiji with Los Angeles, San Francisco and Honolulu, with Nadi serving as a key hub for travellers from Australia, New Zealand and other Pacific countries heading to the United States.

Its partnership with American Airlines also provides passengers with onward connections to destinations across the US.

The expanded regulatory authority comes as Fiji Airways adjusts parts of its international network in response to changing market conditions and operating costs.

The new authorization gives Fiji Airways greater scope to expand its US operations in the future, but any new services would depend on the airline’s commercial and network decisions.

For now, the carrier appears focused on consolidating its existing network while maintaining the flexibility to pursue further opportunities in the American market.

item.title: COMPOL Tudravu to recruits: Toe the line or leave
item.description: Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu has issued a firm warning to 185 new police recruits that those unable to meet the Fiji Police Force’s standards of discipline will not make it through their six-month training. Opening the Batch 70 Basic Recruit Course at the Fiji Police Academy yesterday, Mr Tudravu stressed that discipline would be non-negotiable throughout the training.
item.content:encoded:
Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu has issued a firm warning to 185 new police recruits that those unable to meet the Fiji Police Force’s standards of discipline will not make it through their six-month training.

Opening the Batch 70 Basic Recruit Course at the Fiji Police Academy yesterday, Mr Tudravu stressed that discipline would be non-negotiable throughout the training.

“If you cannot toe the line, the gates remain open, and you have seen that I have been serious about this from the moment you marched in,” Mr Tudravu told the recruits.

“Let’s get rid of the bad apples and ensure only the cream of the crop will march out at the end of the six months.”

The Commissioner said he expected the best from the recruits and wanted future officers who were physically and mentally capable of dealing with the challenges they would encounter on the frontline.

He reminded them that policing was not simply about acquiring technical knowledge and skills, but also about developing character, leadership and the right attitude towards the communities they would serve.

“Your training here is not just about acquiring policing knowledge and skills, but also about developing the character, leadership qualities, and community-focused mindset required to serve the people of Fiji and Tuvalu effectively,” he said.

Mr Tudravu also welcomed 14 recruits from Tuvalu and encouraged them to regard the Fiji Police Academy as their home during the training period.

He told the recruits their conduct would be expected to reflect the standards of the organisation both on and off duty.

“This means your every action, your every being, from the way you talk to people, on or off duty, the way you treat your work, must always be aligned to the organizational mission and vision,” Mr Tudravu said.

“Anything less is a disservice to your oath, the police uniform and organization.”

The six-month training for Batch 70 is scheduled to conclude on February 12, 2027.

item.title: Auditor-General flags governance failures across municipal councils
item.description: The Auditor-General has raised serious concerns over financial reporting, governance and internal controls across Fiji’s municipal councils after modified audit opinions were issued on all 19 financial statements audited. In its Report on Municipal Councils, the Auditor-General said the findings reflected negatively on the councils and required urgent attention from those responsible for their gov
item.content:encoded:
The Auditor-General has raised serious concerns over financial reporting, governance and internal controls across Fiji’s municipal councils after modified audit opinions were issued on all 19 financial statements audited.

In its Report on Municipal Councils, the Auditor-General said the findings reflected negatively on the councils and required urgent attention from those responsible for their governance.

This report includes the audit results of 19 financial statements for 8 Municipal Councils as follows:

-Nausori Town Council 2019 to 2021 -Tavua Town Council 2021 to 2023 -Rakiraki Town Council 2024 & 2025 -Levuka Town Council 2019 -Savusavu Town Council 2018 to 2020 -Suva City Council 2020 -Labasa Town Council 2019 to 2021 -Lami Town Council 2021 to 2023

“Urgent attention should be given to address matters which have been highlighted in the Auditors’ Reports,” the report stated.

A major concern identified was the quality and timeliness of financial reporting, with delays in submitting financial statements preventing the Auditor-General from providing Parliament and other stakeholders with timely audit findings.

“Improving the quality and timeliness of financial reporting is a major concern that needs to be addressed by those charged with governance of the Municipal Councils,” the report said.

The audit also found weaknesses in governance and internal controls, with some regulations, formal policies and procedures either outdated or non-existent.

“Good governance and internal controls are lacking because regulations, formal policies and procedures to govern all aspects of the Municipal Councils’ operations were not reviewed and updated for a long period of time or that they do not exist,” the report stated.

Poor records management was another concern, with the Auditor-General noting missing financial records and the absence of a policy specifically addressing effective records management.

The report recommended that improving financial statements be treated as an “utmost priority”, including employing suitably qualified accountants capable of preparing financial statements on time.

It also recommended establishing a robust audit, risk and improvement committee to address financial reporting, governance and internal control deficiencies.

Municipal councils were further urged to maintain accurate fixed-asset records and develop clear plans for asset valuations.

“The Ministry of Local Government should continue to strengthen its monitoring role on the operations of the Municipal Councils to improve financial accountability,” the Auditor-General said.

item.title: FHTA welcomes Government shift on tourism tax
item.description: The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has welcomed Government’s decision to exempt existing bookings from the new Tourism Services Tax, describing the change as the outcome the industry had sought since consultations began. Government has confirmed that the five per cent TST will apply only to bookings made on or after September 1, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has welcomed Government’s decision to exempt existing bookings from the new Tourism Services Tax, describing the change as the outcome the industry had sought since consultations began.

Government has confirmed that the five per cent TST will apply only to bookings made on or after September 1, 2026.

This means bookings made before that date will not attract the tax, even if the tourism service is provided after September 1.

FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said the decision removed uncertainty for visitors who had booked and paid for their Fiji holidays months before the tax was due to take effect.

“This is a genuinely welcome result, and the right one,” Ms Lockington said.

“It restores fairness for visitors who planned their holiday in good faith, and it removes a real source of confusion and the higher risk of booking cancellations for the industry.”

She also acknowledged Government’s stated commitment to listening to the tourism industry and working collaboratively on policies supporting sustainable economic growth.

FHTA had consistently pushed for existing bookings to be exempt, arguing that visitors should not face an additional tax that did not exist when they booked their holidays.

Despite welcoming the change, the association said further clarity was still needed before implementation.

FHTA is awaiting updated Standard Interpretation Guidelines and further guidance from the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service on the scope and application of the tax.

“While not complete in terms of the clarity around the application, we are absolutely delighted with the outcome,” Ms Lockington said.

“Members still need clear, practical answers before 1 September.”

She said FHTA would continue working with FRCS despite the increasingly limited time available for tourism businesses to update their systems.

The five per cent TST will apply for 12 months from September 1, 2026, to specified tourism businesses with annual turnover of $2 million or more and to specified tourism services.

item.title: Fiji Airways to stop direct Canberra-Nadi flights, Canberra Times reports
item.description: Fiji Airways will suspend its direct flights between Canberra and Nadi early next year, citing challenging market conditions. According to a report by The Canberra Times , Fiji Airways informed affected passengers that the service would be suspended from February 5, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways will suspend its direct flights between Canberra and Nadi early next year, citing challenging market conditions.

According to a report by The Canberra Times , Fiji Airways informed affected passengers that the service would be suspended from February 5, 2027.

“Due to market conditions, we have taken the difficult decision to suspend our Canberra to Nadi services effective 5th February 2027,” the airline reportedly told a passenger booked to travel after that date.

Fiji Airways told The Canberra Times that travellers from Canberra would still be able to reach Fiji through its daily Sydney-Nadi services, which it said were already used by many Canberra passengers.

The airline described the decision as a suspension but did not provide a date for the route’s possible resumption.

The Canberra-Nadi route was launched three years ago with considerable fanfare and initially operated three times a week.

Canberra Airport Head of Aviation Michael Thomson said global uncertainty, rising aviation fuel prices and weaker demand for travel to the United States had affected the viability of the service.

“The impacts of global uncertainty, continued escalation of fuel prices and softer demand for travel to the United States have currently made the service challenging to sustain,” Mr Thomson told The Canberra Times .

He described Fiji Airways’ decision as disappointing but expressed hope the airline would eventually return.

“We thank Fiji Airways for its commitment to Canberra and look forward to welcoming them back when the economic conditions improve,” he said.

Mr Thomson said Canberra Airport remained focused on expanding direct international connectivity for the region.

Fiji Airways’ withdrawal will bring an end, at least temporarily, to Canberra’s direct air connection with Nadi, requiring Fiji-bound passengers to consider connecting services, including through Sydney.
